After Teaching | Spring 2026

After working through the full lesson sequence with your students, you now have a richer picture of how the layering process unfolded, including what supported learning, where students faced challenges, and what shifted in their thinking. This discussion is a space to reflect on the arc of the experience, to name what you learned as a teacher-researcher, and to consider how this process might shape your teaching moving forward. Your reflections help deepen our collective understanding of what layered reading, writing, and discussion make possible for young writers.


This is the third of the three connected discussions in this module. Completing all three (before, during, and after teaching) allows you to earn the discussion badge for Module 4.

💬 Reflect and Share

Now that you have taught the full lesson sequence with students, join the After Teaching discussion and share your reflection on the experience for your and your students.

If it helps, use one or more of the sentence stems below to reflect on your overall experience with this lesson sequence.

  • I was surprised when. . .

  • I got stuck when _________, so I decided to. . .

  • I was proud when. . .

As you celebrate with your students, please share samples, pictures, and/or video snippets with our community. The work does not have to be final or complete. Post what you observed during the lessons to help us enter your classroom with you and your learners: Kid language, questions, misconceptions, a-ha’s, and student thinking.

Be sure to take a few minutes to respond to at least two other teachers’ posts to continue the conversation.

As a final step in this module, you’ll connect with your facilitator to reflect more deeply on what you learned. While the discussions gave you space to share along the way, this reflection is a chance to step back, consider the implications for your teaching, and think about what you might want to explore next.

➡️ Teacher as Researcher Final Reflection


Micro Credential

Teacher as Researcher | Sustaining Literacy Routines

This badge recognizes your participation in a shared teacher-research cycle by preparing, teaching, and reflecting on the Layered Writing lesson sequence with colleagues.

Student Writing for April Regroup Meeting

As you complete this module, plan to gather 10–12 student drafts from the Layered Writing lesson sequence to bring to the Spring Regroup Meeting on April 9th. Choose a range of student work—not just the strongest pieces—to help capture how different students engaged with the task.

These drafts do not need to be final. Early, in-progress writing is ideal for the collaborative analysis we’ll do together, as we look for patterns in student thinking, notice writing moves students are beginning to take up, and consider instructional next steps. The goal is not polished products, but insight into students’ thinking as it develops.

I really liked using this with my 8th graders. I found that I really needed to look at the lesson sequence to keep track of each step. I got a little ahead of myself at one point because I was excited and ready to move at a fast pace. I learned that this is a slower is better exercise. I also ended up doing a Thursday/Friday, Monday/Tuesday and I was concerned but I actually think the spaced practice worked in my favor. Students were intrigued by the content and actually retained information from day to day. Plus, it is inherently chunked so each step was bite size and avoided cognitive overload-which I think is a frequent issue I see in writing and research and synthesis of multiple texts. Students enjoyed the layers and connected the activities well. I sometimes get students who disconnect what we do day to day, but I think the visual of seeing the writing and image all flowing together on the page helped them keep it connected in their own minds. I liked this a lot and will definitely use it in the future!

I was surprised how well this worked with my students. By breaking up the texts, the students weren't overwhelmed. We worked on one text per day followed by a the writing that goes with that text because we were stuck with the time constraint of 50 minute class periods. By the fourth day they were ready to fill out their graphic organizer easier than they have in the past when they looked for information from many sources that I didn't provide for them. When the began their writing they were able to go back to cite the information with little difficulty. I was proud of my students when they produced their writing, even my reluctant writer.

Stephanie Beadle

I feel like this was a great activity to model how to use sources and create an argument. I'd like to do this earlier in the school year, before we've done some of the other writing tasks, but I also think this was a great scaffolding activity before a larger research project. I can use the language about entering, exploring, mapping, and joining the conversation as their own research texts start to emerge. I let my students choose their topic, and two classes chose school start times and two chose fast fashion. I think school start times was a far more engaging topic that they connected to more fully. So I could actually see doing this with that topic earlier in the school year and then once they have some confidence with the framework, moving into things like Fast Fashion that they don't have as much prior knowledge and experience with. I loved seeing them engage with share-connect-share and it was also a great idea to have them move to someone they hadn't talked to yet to share their visual. I also enjoyed watching them struggle with the visual, and then come up with some really interesting and thoughtful ideas! This activity also helped me see who needs some more help with reasoning and argument.

To be honest, I was surprised when the students actually engaged with this. I thought they would all hate 3 days of reading, talking and writing. Many did say 3 days was a lot, but it wasn't that bad. They actually learned the material and felt better informed. I had the students complete a survey on their thoughts about the layered writing and the responses were mostly positive and students thought I should do it again next year.

  • I was proud when students figured things out for themselves. When I told them to create a visual to represent all the texts, many initially panicked but after a minute they started drawing. Once they started they took off. It was even better when I told them to add themselves to the conversation. Watching them try to figure out how to include themselves in their visual was great. I was surprised by the different representations. Many people made themselves stick figured in their drawings, but some became thermometers to show their feelings on the issues, etc. The visuals were creative and there wasn't much complaining.

  • Overall, there wasn't much complaining- which is great. They seemed to like that they could chat with friends. They were willing to do the quick writes after that. (I timed the writing and that seemed to help.). All of the structure helped make their final argument writing good. The students had supported opinions and I could tell they were thinking. It was great!

Overall, I am pleased with this lesson! The group I did it with this time is a much more difficult group than my others, yet they had incredible discussions and I love how beneficial it was for my struggling readers. When performing the activity as the student on the Zoom call, I enjoyed how deeply I was prompted to synthesize the information, but I did not predict the benefit to struggling readers when doing this activity in a group setting. It beautifully differentiated the content so that my advanced learners were able to push themselves to deep understanding, and my struggling readers were able to gently lean on those group discussions to make the text accessible for their own understanding. I LOVED the ah-ha moments my struggling learners had when they finally felt prepared to join the conversation and all the content came together for them. I noticed that each text got easier for my struggling readers as they built an understanding of the topic. Next time, I will begin with an easier text and progressively increase the rigor of the texts.

Leigh A Rogers
9:38 am

Now that I have gone through the full lesson sequence, I am so excited to start thinking about how I will refine this assignment for next year. I loved this lesson sequence because it not only taught students to really consider counter arguments, but it also taught them to really listen to the nuances within an argument. For my lower level readers, they struggled a bit with noticing shifts in the conversation. They largely lumped all of the texts together and said they were the same. It wasn’t until I was able to sit down with these students and show them how to identify the claim and supporting points that they were able to see how the argument differed between sources. These misreadings showed me that I need to take more time in having students summarize and potentially outline a speaker’s points. I will admit that I have spent years devaluing the importance of students summarizing an author’s ideas because that instruction felt largely elementary and middle-school to me. However, I realize that many of my students struggle to break down what a text is actually saying unless they do this step first. Summarizing also allows me to quickly assess their reader comprehension. This was one reason I loved the visual element at the end of the layered writing. It was a quick assessment of student reader comprehension. A few additional strategies I would like to use for quick assessment would be summarizing the main idea in one sentence, choosing a quote the student feels really captures the main idea of this piece and explaining how that quote does that, and quick outlining of the author’s argument. 

I am also really looking forward to the writing work we will do together at the Write to Learn Conference. I tried to give my students much more autonomy than I have in the past when it came to the writing assignment. I was inspired by Jennifer Fletcher’s Writing Rhetorically in that I wanted to see what students could do when they only had a class period to produce a piece and could not use me to check their writing. It was a little uncomfortable, and I know it pushed the students who desire more 1:1 feedback at every step of the way, but I also think it was good to teach them this autonomy in writing, especially when we have spent so much time over the course of the year working to understand how to develop strong claims and support those claims with relevant and sufficient evidence. I would like some feedback on my rubric and prompt in addition to looking at student writing to see if I need to be more specific in my rubric or if I need to just grow a little more comfortable with students being uncomfortable. 

I have shared two pictures of students’ notes during the Layered Writing activity. I found these most helpful when it came to assessing student comprehension of the texts. For example, in Student Artifact 4, reading her notes showed me that she had some pretty big misconceptions about the texts. My first alarm was the statement she made that not everyone agreed humans came from apes. I was really confused how she had pulled that conclusion from the piece at all. I went back and watched the video again, and I realized she was most likely pulling this from when the speaker said “humans are animals” relating to a predator-prey instinct. I did also notice there was about a one second clip with a picture showing an ape on the left side growing into a human on the right side. I was able to sit with this student and talk about the importance of not taking one small piece of what someone is saying and ignoring the rest. I was also able to clarify her understanding of opinions. She had mentioned that we’re not supposed to have our opinions in our writing, which allowed me to ask her what persuasive writing was as well as analytical claims and analysis. These were all good conversations, and afterwards, she realized the speaker’s actual claim and was not building everything off of one small portion of the text.

Sarah Apple
12:22 pm

This was a really great side quest for my students between units. I have noticed an uptick in the battles over cell phones and laptop usage in class so I think it provided some time for reflection. The students were very engaged because, of course, they can connect to the conversation around cell phone usage and the impacts of social media. They also are pretty motivated to defend their usage. I staggered the lesson over three days. We introduced the Texts 1 (a video) and 2 (an article) on day one. The next day was a block period - so we spent 90 minutes on 2 more texts (the provided article and I added an additional video). This was the day for a lot of the discussion and writing in notebooks. We did a gallery walk of the visuals they created and had time to revise. The final class period was for writing the argument. I did not specify a length and just encouraged them to be thorough in their argument. The responses varied quite a bit, and I am not surprised. I really like how it scaffolded exploring a topic and the idea of the layered texts being in conversation with each other. A great approach to research and argumentative writing that I plan to incorporate with Claim Evidence Reasoning activities.

I loved seeing them engage with share-connect-share and it was also a great idea to have them move to someone they hadn't talked to yet to share their visual. I also enjoyed watching them struggle with the visual, and then come up with some really interesting and thoughtful ideas! This activity also helped me see who needs some more help with reasoning and argument.

I am with you for doing this in the beginning of the year. My students write "paragraphs of the week." We do five paragraphs over argumentative writing, five paragraphs over informational, and five paragraphs over narrative. This would be great to do before we start our paragraph of the week's over argumentative. This made our argumentative essay work so well this week after doing the layered writing routine. We have been preparing for the MAP so I do plan to make this routine work with narrative and informational writings as well.

Breanna Smith
1:05 pm
Leigh A Rogers

Now that I have gone through the full lesson sequence, I am so excited to start thinking about how I will refine this assignment for next year. I loved this lesson sequence because it not only taught students to really consider counter arguments, but it also taught them to really listen to the nuances within an argument. For my lower level readers, they struggled a bit with noticing shifts in the conversation. They largely lumped all of the texts together and said they were the same. It wasn’t until I was able to sit down with these students and show them how to identify the claim and supporting points that they were able to see how the argument differed between sources. These misreadings showed me that I need to take more time in having students summarize and potentially outline a speaker’s points. I will admit that I have spent years devaluing the importance of students summarizing an author’s ideas because that instruction felt largely elementary and middle-school to me. However, I realize that many of my students struggle to break down what a text is actually saying unless they do this step first. Summarizing also allows me to quickly assess their reader comprehension. This was one reason I loved the visual element at the end of the layered writing. It was a quick assessment of student reader comprehension. A few additional strategies I would like to use for quick assessment would be summarizing the main idea in one sentence, choosing a quote the student feels really captures the main idea of this piece and explaining how that quote does that, and quick outlining of the author’s argument. 

I am also really looking forward to the writing work we will do together at the Write to Learn Conference. I tried to give my students much more autonomy than I have in the past when it came to the writing assignment. I was inspired by Jennifer Fletcher’s Writing Rhetorically in that I wanted to see what students could do when they only had a class period to produce a piece and could not use me to check their writing. It was a little uncomfortable, and I know it pushed the students who desire more 1:1 feedback at every step of the way, but I also think it was good to teach them this autonomy in writing, especially when we have spent so much time over the course of the year working to understand how to develop strong claims and support those claims with relevant and sufficient evidence. I would like some feedback on my rubric and prompt in addition to looking at student writing to see if I need to be more specific in my rubric or if I need to just grow a little more comfortable with students being uncomfortable. 

I have shared two pictures of students’ notes during the Layered Writing activity. I found these most helpful when it came to assessing student comprehension of the texts. For example, in Student Artifact 4, reading her notes showed me that she had some pretty big misconceptions about the texts. My first alarm was the statement she made that not everyone agreed humans came from apes. I was really confused how she had pulled that conclusion from the piece at all. I went back and watched the video again, and I realized she was most likely pulling this from when the speaker said “humans are animals” relating to a predator-prey instinct. I did also notice there was about a one second clip with a picture showing an ape on the left side growing into a human on the right side. I was able to sit with this student and talk about the importance of not taking one small piece of what someone is saying and ignoring the rest. I was also able to clarify her understanding of opinions. She had mentioned that we’re not supposed to have our opinions in our writing, which allowed me to ask her what persuasive writing was as well as analytical claims and analysis. These were all good conversations, and afterwards, she realized the speaker’s actual claim and was not building everything off of one small portion of the text. 

This reflection shows a lot of thoughtful growth in your practice. It’s especially insightful how you recognized that summarizing—something that can feel “basic”—is actually essential for helping students access more complex skills like analyzing claims and counterarguments. Your plan to incorporate quick, targeted strategies (like one-sentence summaries and outlining arguments) seems like a strong way to support comprehension without slowing momentum.

I also think your willingness to give students more autonomy, even when it feels uncomfortable, is really valuable. That balance between support and independence is hard to find, but it sounds like you’re helping students build real confidence as writers.

I have shared two pictures of students’ notes during the Layered Writing activity. I found these most helpful when it came to assessing student comprehension of the texts. For example, in Student Artifact 4, reading her notes showed me that she had some pretty big misconceptions about the texts. My first alarm was the statement she made that not everyone agreed humans came from apes. I was really confused how she had pulled that conclusion from the piece at all. I went back and watched the video again, and I realized she was most likely pulling this from when the speaker said “humans are animals” relating to a predator-prey instinct. I did also notice there was about a one second clip with a picture showing an ape on the left side growing into a human on the right side. I was able to sit with this student and talk about the importance of not taking one small piece of what someone is saying and ignoring the rest. I was also able to clarify her understanding of opinions. She had mentioned that we’re not supposed to have our opinions in our writing, which allowed me to ask her what persuasive writing was as well as analytical claims and analysis. These were all good conversations, and afterwards, she realized the speaker’s actual claim and was not building everything off of one small portion of the text. 

I too found that I need to put more emphasis in my instruction on students focusing on texts and really processing what an author is saying. I discovered that, for my 6th graders, I wished I’d done the reading of the articles aloud so they could have focused more in getting the author’s main claim and really understanding the author’s ideas.

Now that I have gone through the full lesson sequence, I am so excited to start thinking about how I will refine this assignment for next year. I loved this lesson sequence because it not only taught students to really consider counter arguments, but it also taught them to really listen to the nuances within an argument. For my lower level readers, they struggled a bit with noticing shifts in the conversation. They largely lumped all of the texts together and said they were the same. It wasn’t until I was able to sit down with these students and show them how to identify the claim and supporting points that they were able to see how the argument differed between sources. These misreadings showed me that I need to take more time in having students summarize and potentially outline a speaker’s points. I will admit that I have spent years devaluing the importance of students summarizing an author’s ideas because that instruction felt largely elementary and middle-school to me. However, I realize that many of my students struggle to break down what a text is actually saying unless they do this step first. Summarizing also allows me to quickly assess their reader comprehension. This was one reason I loved the visual element at the end of the layered writing. It was a quick assessment of student reader comprehension. A few additional strategies I would like to use for quick assessment would be summarizing the main idea in one sentence, choosing a quote the student feels really captures the main idea of this piece and explaining how that quote does that, and quick outlining of the author’s argument.

I tried to give my students much more autonomy than I have in the past when it came to the writing assignment. I was inspired by Jennifer Fletcher’s Writing Rhetorically in that I wanted to see what students could do when they only had a class period to produce a piece and could not use me to check their writing. In the first article, it talked about how human activities like cutting down forests and building cities are a big reason species become endangered. That made me feel like we have a responsibility to fix what we caused.

After reading the second article, I started to see how people are already trying to help, like making laws and protecting areas where animals live. I also thought it was interesting that saving one species can help other parts of the ecosystem. That made me think helping animals can have a bigger positive impact than I realized.

But the third article made me think more about the downsides. It said that some laws can cause problems for people, like landowners, and that sometimes focusing on just one species might not fix the bigger issue. That made me question if helping is always the best choice.

Now I think humans should help endangered species, but not in every situation. We should focus more on fixing the environment as a whole instead of just one animal at a time. I still think we have a responsibility, but we need to be smarter about how we help.

I really enjoyed every step of this writing strategy, and I told my students over and over how improvement could be seen even within the 3-4 days it took us to complete the work. Overall, most of my students rose to the challenge of layered reading and writing, and they approached the work with 100% effort. They worked hard to understand the informational passages, and they asked so many good questions about words and concepts they weren't sure about. Even some of my most reluctant readers asked questions, wanting to fully understand what they were reading. I did see a lot of blank stares when we reached the third layer, and the students had to create a visual representation of the three articles. Several examples later, everyone was engaged and was trying to come up with the perfect drawing. For future lessons, I know now to have more examples of exactly what a visual representation might mean. Another important learning moment came from my co-teaching classes. I found that providing them with sentence stems before their writing began in the last layer was essential in helping students stay focused. I don't think these particular groups of kids would have been able to keep the writing portion organized enough to make sense of it all if they hadn't had those. The template that another teacher and I made was also very helpful and really helped the kids stay organized throughout the layers. It also allowed for each of them to be able to see all of their work in one place, making the final piece of writing easier.

Leigh A Rogers

Now that I have gone through the full lesson sequence, I am so excited to start thinking about how I will refine this assignment for next year. I loved this lesson sequence because it not only taught students to really consider counter arguments, but it also taught them to really listen to the nuances within an argument. For my lower level readers, they struggled a bit with noticing shifts in the conversation. They largely lumped all of the texts together and said they were the same. It wasn’t until I was able to sit down with these students and show them how to identify the claim and supporting points that they were able to see how the argument differed between sources. These misreadings showed me that I need to take more time in having students summarize and potentially outline a speaker’s points. I will admit that I have spent years devaluing the importance of students summarizing an author’s ideas because that instruction felt largely elementary and middle-school to me. However, I realize that many of my students struggle to break down what a text is actually saying unless they do this step first. Summarizing also allows me to quickly assess their reader comprehension. This was one reason I loved the visual element at the end of the layered writing. It was a quick assessment of student reader comprehension. A few additional strategies I would like to use for quick assessment would be summarizing the main idea in one sentence, choosing a quote the student feels really captures the main idea of this piece and explaining how that quote does that, and quick outlining of the author’s argument. 

I am also really looking forward to the writing work we will do together at the Write to Learn Conference. I tried to give my students much more autonomy than I have in the past when it came to the writing assignment. I was inspired by Jennifer Fletcher’s Writing Rhetorically in that I wanted to see what students could do when they only had a class period to produce a piece and could not use me to check their writing. It was a little uncomfortable, and I know it pushed the students who desire more 1:1 feedback at every step of the way, but I also think it was good to teach them this autonomy in writing, especially when we have spent so much time over the course of the year working to understand how to develop strong claims and support those claims with relevant and sufficient evidence. I would like some feedback on my rubric and prompt in addition to looking at student writing to see if I need to be more specific in my rubric or if I need to just grow a little more comfortable with students being uncomfortable. 

I have shared two pictures of students’ notes during the Layered Writing activity. I found these most helpful when it came to assessing student comprehension of the texts. For example, in Student Artifact 4, reading her notes showed me that she had some pretty big misconceptions about the texts. My first alarm was the statement she made that not everyone agreed humans came from apes. I was really confused how she had pulled that conclusion from the piece at all. I went back and watched the video again, and I realized she was most likely pulling this from when the speaker said “humans are animals” relating to a predator-prey instinct. I did also notice there was about a one second clip with a picture showing an ape on the left side growing into a human on the right side. I was able to sit with this student and talk about the importance of not taking one small piece of what someone is saying and ignoring the rest. I was also able to clarify her understanding of opinions. She had mentioned that we’re not supposed to have our opinions in our writing, which allowed me to ask her what persuasive writing was as well as analytical claims and analysis. These were all good conversations, and afterwards, she realized the speaker’s actual claim and was not building everything off of one small portion of the text. 

I really related when you said, "I will admit that I have spent years devaluing the importance of students summarizing an author’s ideas because that instruction felt largely elementary and middle-school to me." I too struggle with that. It feels too simple or like the easy way out. However, when I remember it helps with reading comp as well, I think, "Hey, i've got to be hitting at least 2 priority standards, right?'

For future lessons, I know now to have more examples of exactly what a visual representation might mean. Another important learning moment came from my co-teaching classes. I found that providing them with sentence stems before their writing began in the last layer was essential in helping students stay focused. I don't think these particular groups of kids would have been able to keep the writing portion organized enough to make sense of it all if they hadn't had those. The template that another teacher and I made was also very helpful and really helped the kids stay organized throughout the layers. It also allowed for each of them to be able to see all of their work in one place, making the final piece of writing easier.

Sentence stems for the win! I'm also going to offer more structured vocab support for some of the articles next year and give the students the opportunity to interact with the vocab, beyond just annotating and summarizing.

This experience helped me reflect on both my students’ learning and my own growth as a teacher. I was most proud when I saw students begin using evidence from the text to support their claims, since this was something they struggled with at first. When we started the topic of later school start times, most students had a simple opinion. But as they read more and talked through the ideas, their thinking became deeper. By the third reading, they were considering how start times connect to responsibility and healthy habits.

We have also just begun pushing into writing in this way, and students are starting to see the value of it. They are learning that gaining knowledge from more than one source helps them better understand a topic and find evidence that supports their thinking.

I also learned how important it is to break learning into smaller steps. The handout with guiding questions helped students get started, and our class discussions helped them think more deeply. The combination of reading, writing, and discussion really helped students grow as writers.

One challenge during this research was student absences, which made it difficult for some students to stay consistent with the process. In addition, having a student teacher during this time created some adjustments in instruction and continuity. Despite these challenges, the overall growth in student thinking and writing was still clear.

As a teacher, my biggest takeaway is to connect this kind of work to my subject. Since I teach history, I would use topics that match what we are learning in class. This would save time and keep students focused on important content. Moving forward, I plan to continue using reading, writing, and discussion together to help students become stronger thinkers and writers.

Leigh A Rogers

Now that I have gone through the full lesson sequence, I am so excited to start thinking about how I will refine this assignment for next year. I loved this lesson sequence because it not only taught students to really consider counter arguments, but it also taught them to really listen to the nuances within an argument. For my lower level readers, they struggled a bit with noticing shifts in the conversation. They largely lumped all of the texts together and said they were the same. It wasn’t until I was able to sit down with these students and show them how to identify the claim and supporting points that they were able to see how the argument differed between sources. These misreadings showed me that I need to take more time in having students summarize and potentially outline a speaker’s points. I will admit that I have spent years devaluing the importance of students summarizing an author’s ideas because that instruction felt largely elementary and middle-school to me. However, I realize that many of my students struggle to break down what a text is actually saying unless they do this step first. Summarizing also allows me to quickly assess their reader comprehension. This was one reason I loved the visual element at the end of the layered writing. It was a quick assessment of student reader comprehension. A few additional strategies I would like to use for quick assessment would be summarizing the main idea in one sentence, choosing a quote the student feels really captures the main idea of this piece and explaining how that quote does that, and quick outlining of the author’s argument. 

I am also really looking forward to the writing work we will do together at the Write to Learn Conference. I tried to give my students much more autonomy than I have in the past when it came to the writing assignment. I was inspired by Jennifer Fletcher’s Writing Rhetorically in that I wanted to see what students could do when they only had a class period to produce a piece and could not use me to check their writing. It was a little uncomfortable, and I know it pushed the students who desire more 1:1 feedback at every step of the way, but I also think it was good to teach them this autonomy in writing, especially when we have spent so much time over the course of the year working to understand how to develop strong claims and support those claims with relevant and sufficient evidence. I would like some feedback on my rubric and prompt in addition to looking at student writing to see if I need to be more specific in my rubric or if I need to just grow a little more comfortable with students being uncomfortable. 

I have shared two pictures of students’ notes during the Layered Writing activity. I found these most helpful when it came to assessing student comprehension of the texts. For example, in Student Artifact 4, reading her notes showed me that she had some pretty big misconceptions about the texts. My first alarm was the statement she made that not everyone agreed humans came from apes. I was really confused how she had pulled that conclusion from the piece at all. I went back and watched the video again, and I realized she was most likely pulling this from when the speaker said “humans are animals” relating to a predator-prey instinct. I did also notice there was about a one second clip with a picture showing an ape on the left side growing into a human on the right side. I was able to sit with this student and talk about the importance of not taking one small piece of what someone is saying and ignoring the rest. I was also able to clarify her understanding of opinions. She had mentioned that we’re not supposed to have our opinions in our writing, which allowed me to ask her what persuasive writing was as well as analytical claims and analysis. These were all good conversations, and afterwards, she realized the speaker’s actual claim and was not building everything off of one small portion of the text. 

Leigh, I think the realization that students struggle to break down discussions is relatable! I sometimes assume my MS/HS students have a skill only to learn they really do not. It is also nice to have an approach that allows the lower-skilled students to access more difficult texts alongside the more skilled readers and writers.
